name: Quantum Advantage Defined
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Fast at Something Real, Not Just Something Hard
lesson.summary: Quantum advantage raises the bar past quantum supremacy by asking for a speedup on a problem people actually care about, a bar that has arguably never been cleanly and durably cleared.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter defined quantum supremacy as beating the best classical computer at some specific task, with no requirement that the task matter to anyone. Quantum advantage is the term much of the field now reaches for to name the harder, more meaningful claim: a quantum computer outperforming classical computers on a problem that has genuine practical value, whether that is a chemistry simulation relevant to drug design, an optimization problem relevant to logistics, or some other task people would actually want solved regardless of which kind of computer solves it. In practice the two terms are used inconsistently across papers and press releases, some authors treat them as synonyms, others use supremacy specifically for artificial, contrived tasks and advantage specifically for useful ones, so it is worth reading any specific claim carefully rather than assuming which definition is in play.

Why does this distinction matter so much to a skeptic? Because it is one thing to build a quantum processor that wins at a game designed to be unwinnable for classical computers, and quite another to build one that outperforms decades of classical algorithmic refinement on a problem industry or science actually needs solved. The first has been claimed, contested, and partially walked back multiple times, as covered in the previous chapter on quantum supremacy. The second, a clean, durable, and broadly accepted demonstration of quantum advantage on a genuinely useful problem, has arguably never been fully achieved as of this writing. Several claimed instances, across superconducting and photonic hardware, have followed the same pattern seen with Sycamore: an initial announcement of a large classical to quantum gap, followed within months or a few years by improved classical algorithms, smarter approximations, or more efficient classical hardware use that substantially closed or eliminated the claimed gap.

This is not a story of quantum computing being fake, it is a story of the comparison being a genuinely moving target. Classical computing is not a fixed baseline sitting still waiting to be beaten, it is an actively improving field with enormous existing investment, and any claim of quantum advantage has to keep beating classical methods that keep getting better in response to the challenge. That dynamic is part of why serious researchers in the field have become more cautious about declaring quantum advantage achieved and more careful to specify exactly which classical baseline was used, for how long it was tested, and whether the comparison holds up under further classical optimization.

None of this erases the theoretical promise established by algorithms like Shor's and Grover's, both of which rest on rigorous mathematical proofs of speedup that do not depend on the current state of classical algorithm engineering the way empirical advantage claims do. What it does mean is that empirical claims of advantage, made about specific hardware running specific tasks today, deserve the same scrutiny as any other extraordinary claim, and that scrutiny is exactly what the next chapter turns toward.
